charts.annotation: Automobile's EV-strategy reversal (~¥1,577.8bn of charges in FY2026, a further ~¥485bn in H1 FY2027) shows up here as segment losses even while Motorcycle stays highly profitable.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
Honda discloses revenue for four segments: Automobile (unit sales of cars/light trucks), Financial Services (captive finance and leasing income supporting those sales), Motorcycle (high-volume two-wheelers, led by Asia/India) and Power Products & Other (small engines, HondaJet).

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: Automobile is ~64% of revenue and the largest swing factor; Motorcycle is only ~18% of revenue but carries the business on profit (see Operating Profit by Segment). Only quarterly data is disclosed for the segment split -- FY/annual rows are intentionally blank, not missing.

What to watch:

  • Automobile unit-revenue trend as North American tariffs and the hybrid pivot play out
  • Financial Services receivables growth (+11% YoY in FY2026) as a leading indicator of auto volume

segmentProfit.title: Operating profit by segment
segmentProfit.content:
Segment operating profit, reported alongside segment revenue, is where Honda's four businesses diverge most: a segment can grow revenue while losing money, or vice versa.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: Automobile swung to losses in FY2026 and H1 FY2027 on EV-strategy reversal charges (cancelled US EV models, scaled-back North American EV production, Sony Honda Mobility/Afeela cancellations) and US tariff costs, while Motorcycle posted record profit on +7% unit growth. A blended company-wide margin would hide this entirely.

What to watch:

  • Whether Automobile returns to profit as management targets eliminating EV-related losses and an all-time-high operating profit over FY2027-FY2029
  • Motorcycle profit durability if Automobile needs it to subsidise the EV/hybrid retooling capex

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Honda Motor Co., Ltd.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
